title: Bidirectional Dijkstra: Faster Paths in Excelsior!
description: Watch Bidirectional Dijkstra shrink search space by expanding from both start and goal until the frontiers meet. This reel visualizes how real street-like graphs can be routed efficiently with weighted shortest paths.
ig_caption:
🗺️⚡ Excelsior street grids, but make it math: **Bidirectional Dijkstra**! 

How it works (the deep technical bit 🧠): instead of running one Dijkstra from the start, we run **two** coordinated Dijkstra searches—one forward from the source and one backward from the destination—on a weighted graph (nodes = intersections, edges = street segments). Each side maintains its own priority queue (min-heap) and distance labels, and the algorithm stops when the searches **meet** with an optimal connection (using the best combined frontier cost), drastically reducing explored nodes compared to a single-source approach.

📍Graph theory on real-world maps: even when streets aren’t perfectly uniform, the method still respects **edge weights** (distance/time/cost) and leverages the shortest-path optimality of Dijkstra’s relaxation. On a map-inspired graph of the neighborhood, you can literally see the wavefronts converge like two searchlights finding the quickest crossover.

yt_description:
San Francisco (Excelsior) pathfinding visualization with **Bidirectional Dijkstra** 🚗💨

In this video, we compute shortest paths on a weighted graph inspired by real street maps (nodes/intersections + edges/street segments). Watch how **two Dijkstra frontiers**—one from the start and one from the goal—expand using priority queues and stop when the searches meet at the optimal combined cost.

Keywords: bidirectional dijkstra, pathfinding visualization, shortest path, dijkstra algorithm, graph search, computer science, grid map routing, weighted graphs.

Mechanics: priority queue expansion → relaxation → frontier meeting → shortest path reconstruction.
